sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: This is actually one of the biggest milestones we've reached.
We've completed the entire Financial Core before touching Operations.
That means Projects, Tasks, and Service Tickets won't just be operational modules—they'll be financially aware from day one.

sections.title: Phase 5 — Operations
paragraphs: This phase will become the execution engine of the ERP.
This creates a complete business loop.

sections.title: Phase 5 Roadmap
paragraphs: Although there are only three entities listed, each one is significantly larger than most entities we've built so far because they integrate with nearly every module.

sections.title: Before We Start
paragraphs: Let's define what "Operations" means in KoreVity.
lists: How much time has been spent?

sections.title: Operations Architecture
paragraphs: Notice how Operations now naturally connects into the Financial Core we just built.

sections.title: Why We Didn't Build This Earlier
paragraphs: Now we can do things like:
We couldn't have done that before because Budget, Cost Center, Journal Entries, and the General Ledger didn't exist yet.

sections.title: First Entity — Project
paragraphs: A Project is not just a folder for tasks.
It is the highest operational business container.
Think of it as the operational equivalent of a Customer or Sales Order—but much broader.

sections.title: Project Will Integrate With
paragraphs: This is why Project is one of the largest entities in any ERP.

sections.title: One Architectural Decision Before We Begin
paragraphs: There are two common ways to model Projects.

sections.title: Option A — Simple
paragraphs: Suitable for small project management tools.

sections.title: Option B — Enterprise
paragraphs: This is how enterprise systems are designed.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: We should build Project using the enterprise model from the beginning.
Not because every customer will use every feature immediately, but because:
A small company can ignore Phases and Subtasks.
A large company can use all three.
lists: It scales from a five-person company to a multinational organization.
Features can be enabled gradually without changing the data model.

sections.title: Next Step
paragraphs: This will likely become one of the richest entities in KoreVity because it sits at the intersection of:
It is one of the central business objects of the entire ERP, and we'll design it with the same level of depth as we did for Sales and Finance.
We're now entering one of the largest and most interconnected entities in the entire ERP.
If Customer represents who you work for,
and Sales Order represents what they bought,
then Project represents how the work gets delivered.
This is the operational center of KoreVity.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Project is not a collection of Tasks.
A Project is a business commitment.
The project exists because the business committed to delivering an outcome.

sections.title: A Project is a structured business initiative that organizes work, people, schedules, costs, resources, risks, and financial performance toward achieving a defined business objective.
Relationships
paragraphs: Project becomes one of the most connected entities.

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: Completed projects cannot accept new tasks.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: AI becomes a true project assistant.
"Project Alpha is projected to finish 11 days late because infrastructure tasks are consistently slipping."
lists: Which manager has the highest completion rate?
Which customer projects are least profitable?

sections.title: Projects Should Never Contain Tasks Directly in the Data Model
paragraphs: Because a five-year implementation may contain thousands of tasks.

sections.title: Projects Should Own Financial Performance, Not Accounting
paragraphs: But those values should always be derived from:
The Project should never become another accounting ledger.
It is the consumer of financial information, not its owner.

sections.title: Project as the Operational Hub
paragraphs: It becomes the operational hub of the ERP.

sections.title: Engineering Summary
paragraphs: Project is not a task list.
lists: The central execution entity of the Operations phase.

sections.title: 🏛️ A Significant Architectural Insight
paragraphs: Project is the first entity that truly bridges every major domain of KoreVity.

Unlike Sales Orders, which conclude after fulfillment, Projects are long-lived operational entities. They coordinate work across departments while continuously consuming and producing information from nearly every subsystem we've designed.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Task.
Tasks are the atomic units of work.
Everything measurable inside a Project—progress, effort, time, delays, dependencies, assignments, and eventually Service Tickets—will ultimately be built on Tasks.
If Projects define what the organization has committed to deliver, Tasks define how that commitment is actually executed.
This is where work actually happens.

sections.title: Tasks do.
paragraphs: If the Project is the mission,
This is the execution engine of the ERP.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Task is not a checklist item.
It is a managed unit of work.
A Task is an operational object.

sections.title: A Task is an assignable unit of work within a Project that represents a specific deliverable, activity, or responsibility tracked through planning, execution, completion, and performance measurement.
Responsibilities
paragraphs: It does not own the project.

sections.title: Relationships
paragraphs: Every Task belongs to one Project.

sections.title: Parent Task
paragraphs: Two or three levels are sufficient.

sections.title: Description
paragraphs: A task isn't complete until they are met.

sections.title: Dependencies
paragraphs: One of the most important features.

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: Every Task belongs to one Project.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: "Three blocked infrastructure tasks are delaying eleven downstream tasks."

sections.title: Tasks Should Never Store Time Directly
paragraphs: Time deserves its own entity later.

sections.title: Engineering Summary
paragraphs: Task is not a checklist item.
lists: The execution engine of the ERP.

sections.title: 🏗️ A Major Architectural Insight
paragraphs: With Projects and Tasks complete, KoreVity now has a true work execution model.
This means Projects don't need to micromanage execution—they simply aggregate operational reality from their Tasks.
lists: Time and costs accumulate against Tasks.
Project progress is derived from Task progress.

sections.title: One Refinement I'd Make
paragraphs: I would avoid allowing arbitrary status transitions.
without an explicit reopen action, keeping operational history clean and auditable.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Service Ticket.
Projects and Tasks manage planned work.
The key architectural relationship will be:
That clean separation keeps service management independent while still allowing support work to become structured project execution when needed.
lists: A Service Ticket may create one or more Tasks.
A Task may resolve one or more Service Tickets.

sections.title: Service Ticket as the Service Hub
paragraphs: It becomes the operational hub of service management.

sections.title: Engineering Summary
paragraphs: Service Ticket is not a task.
lists: The foundation of enterprise service management.

sections.title: 🏛️ What We've Built
paragraphs: The Operations layer now forms a complete execution engine.
lists: Service Tickets capture incoming requests and issues.

sections.title: One Architectural Refinement
paragraphs: After completing the Operations Core, I'd introduce a future Time Entry entity.
Instead of storing effort directly on Tasks:

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next major phase should be Human Resources (HR).
Because every major business function is in place.
HR will naturally connect to everything we've built:
The first HR entity should be Employee, because it becomes the human identity that ties together nearly every operational and financial process in KoreVity.
This is one of the most important entities in the entire ERP.
But because almost every other module already references it.
Now we finally define the person behind them.

sections.title: Phase 6 — Human Resources
paragraphs: The HR Core becomes the human layer of the ERP.
If Organizations define where work happens,

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: An Employee is not a User.
This is one of the biggest architectural mistakes many ERP systems make.

sections.title: An Employee is an individual engaged by the organization to perform work, hold organizational responsibilities, participate in operational processes, and contribute to business activities regardless of system access.
Relationships
paragraphs: Employee rapidly becomes one of the most connected entities.

sections.title: Search
paragraphs: One of the most frequently used entities.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: "Sarah currently owns 19 active tasks across four projects and is operating above her average workload."

sections.title: Employees Should Never Store Salary Directly
Engineering Summary
lists: The human foundation of the ERP.

sections.title: 🏛️ A Significant Architectural Insight
paragraphs: Employee is the first entity that represents a person, not a business object.
Keeping these identities separate allows KoreVity to model organizations much more accurately:
Each identity has a distinct purpose while remaining connected where appropriate.
lists: An employee may never log in.
A user may never be an employee.
A customer contact may later become an employee.
An employee may later become a vendor consultant.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Department.
The next step is defining the organizational units those people belong to.
Together, Employee and Department will form the core organizational model upon which the rest of the HR module is built.
Now we move from people to organizational structure.

sections.title: "Where in the organization do they belong?"
paragraphs: This becomes the backbone of reporting, budgeting, approvals, and management.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Department is not a Cost Center.
Many ERP systems incorrectly merge them.

sections.title: A Department is an organizational unit responsible for grouping employees, defining reporting relationships, and organizing business responsibilities within the enterprise.
Parent Department
paragraphs: Three or four levels are sufficient.

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: Archived departments cannot receive new employees.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: "Engineering currently has 42 active employees, 11 projects, and the highest average task workload."
lists: Which department has the highest workload?
Which department has the most open tasks?
Which manager oversees the largest team?

sections.title: Departments Should Not Own Employees
paragraphs: This avoids duplication and simplifies transfers.

sections.title: Department Hierarchies Should Be Recursive
paragraphs: Now organizations of any size are supported without redesign.

sections.title: Engineering Summary
paragraphs: Department is not an accounting object.

sections.title: 🏛️ A Significant Architectural Insight
paragraphs: With Employees and Departments complete, KoreVity now has a complete organizational model.
This hierarchy is independent of Finance.
Keeping those two perspectives separate gives the ERP much greater flexibility.

sections.title: One Refinement I'd Make
paragraphs: After designing this, I'd introduce an optional future concept:
This allows large enterprises to model Teams, Divisions, Offices, and Departments using the same hierarchical framework while preserving Department as the primary HR entity for most organizations.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Position.
An Employee may change over time.
Separating the two makes promotions, transfers, succession planning, and workforce planning much more powerful and much easier to manage.
This is one of the most overlooked concepts in HR systems.
They separate the person from the role.
That single decision makes promotions, transfers, succession planning, and workforce planning dramatically easier.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Position is not an Employee.
A Position exists even when nobody occupies it.

sections.title: A Position is a defined organizational role that specifies responsibilities, authority, reporting relationships, required competencies, and organizational placement independent of the individual occupying it.
Responsibilities
paragraphs: It does not own employment history.

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: Archived positions cannot receive new employees.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: "Engineering currently has three approved Senior Backend Engineer positions that remain vacant."
lists: Which positions are hardest to fill?

sections.title: Position as the Workforce Planning Hub
Engineering Summary
lists: The workforce planning foundation of HR.

sections.title: 🏛️ A Major Architectural Insight
paragraphs: We now have three distinct layers of workforce modeling.
This separation gives KoreVity enterprise-grade flexibility.
Each concept has exactly one responsibility.
lists: A Position can exist before hiring.
An Employee can move to another Position without changing the Position itself.
A Department can be reorganized without altering employee identities.

sections.title: One Refinement I'd Make
paragraphs: I'd allow an Employee to have a Primary Position and optional Secondary Positions.
This supports matrix organizations, temporary assignments, and cross-functional leadership without duplicating employee records.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Employment Agreement.
Now we need to define the legal and contractual relationship between the organization and the employee.

Employment Agreements naturally become the parent for compensation, benefits, probation, contract renewals, and future payroll integration while keeping those changing details separate from the stable Employee record.
Now we move from who the employee is to the legal relationship between the employee and the company.
This is where many HR systems make a mistake.
They put everything on the Employee.
So those things belong somewhere else.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: An Employment Agreement is not an Employee.
An Employee can have multiple Employment Agreements during their career.

sections.title: An Employment Agreement is the formal contractual relationship between an organization and an employee that defines employment terms, working conditions, contractual obligations, compensation framework, and employment lifecycle.
Purpose
paragraphs: Employment Agreements become the foundation for:

sections.title: Responsibilities
paragraphs: It does not own the employee.

sections.title: Reporting Manager
paragraphs: Useful because managers change over time.

sections.title: Relationships
paragraphs: Future HR modules naturally attach here.

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: Only one Active Agreement per employee.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: "Seven contractor agreements expire within the next 45 days."
lists: Which employees are still on probation?

sections.title: Compensation Does NOT Belong Here
paragraphs: The employment agreement remains the legal contract.

sections.title: Employment Agreement as the Legal Hub
Engineering Summary
paragraphs: Employment Agreement is not an employee record.

sections.title: 🏛️ A Major Architectural Insight
paragraphs: We now have four distinct HR layers.
Each layer has a single responsibility.
That separation will make future HR features—Payroll, Leave, Performance, Recruitment, Succession Planning—far easier to build without redesigning the core model.

sections.title: One Refinement I'd Make
paragraphs: I'd also introduce an Agreement Amendment entity in a later phase.
Instead of modifying an active agreement directly:
That preserves the original signed agreement while recording legally traceable changes such as revised working hours, notice periods, or reporting managers.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Compensation.
Now we can define how they are compensated.

Keeping Compensation separate from the Employment Agreement allows salary revisions, bonus plans, allowances, equity, and future payroll calculations to evolve independently while preserving a complete compensation history.
Now we arrive at one of the most sensitive entities in the entire ERP.
Because it contains some of the most confidential business data.
This entity should be designed with security first.
lists: Under which agreement they are employed.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: Compensation is everything the organization provides in exchange for work.

sections.title: Compensation is the structured financial package provided to an employee under an Employment Agreement, consisting of fixed and variable earnings, incentives, allowances, and employer-provided financial benefits.
Allowances
paragraphs: Allowances should become child records later.

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: One Active Compensation per Employment Agreement.

sections.title: Permissions
paragraphs: One of the most restricted entities.
Most employees should never see compensation.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: AI becomes a workforce planning assistant.
"Backend Engineering compensation increased 12% this year, primarily due to market adjustments."
lists: Which departments have the highest compensation growth?

sections.title: Components Should Be Child Records
paragraphs: Now adding new compensation types requires no schema changes.

sections.title: Compensation as the Financial HR Hub
🏛️ A Major Architectural Insight
paragraphs: At this point the HR model is becoming layered exactly like Finance.
Each layer has a single responsibility:
Because these concerns are separated, salary revisions don't require changing contracts, payroll calculations don't modify compensation records, and employment history remains intact.
lists: Payroll (future) = the calculation and payment process.

sections.title: One Refinement I'd Make
paragraphs: I'd introduce a dedicated Compensation Component entity rather than storing bonuses, commissions, and allowances directly on Compensation.
This makes the compensation engine completely configurable and future-proof.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Leave.
Once compensation exists, the next major operational concern is employee availability.
From there we'll have everything needed to model when employees are available, unavailable, and how that affects operations across the ERP.
Now we move from how employees are compensated to when employees are available to work.
This is where HR begins interacting heavily with Operations.
Everything depends on knowing whether someone is actually available.

sections.title: "Was the employee officially excused from work?"
Leave is an approved or recorded period during which an employee is officially absent from work under a defined leave policy and employment agreement.
Responsibilities
paragraphs: It does not own attendance calculations.

sections.title: Relationships
paragraphs: Projects can now anticipate resource availability.

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: Approved leave cannot overlap another approved leave of the same employee.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: "Engineering will have five senior developers on leave during the first week of August, affecting two active projects."
lists: Which departments have staffing shortages next month?
Which projects are affected by upcoming leave?

sections.title: Leave Balance Should Not Be Stored
Separate Leave Policy
paragraphs: Keeping policies separate makes the system globally adaptable.

sections.title: 🏛️ A Major Architectural Insight
paragraphs: The HR model now separates entitlement from usage.

sections.title: One Refinement I'd Make
paragraphs: I'd introduce a dedicated Leave Balance Ledger in a later phase.
Instead of simply calculating balances from requests, every change would be recorded as a transaction.
This mirrors the accounting model we used in Finance and provides a complete, auditable history of every leave balance change.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Attendance.
Leave tells us when someone is officially absent.
Attendance tells us when they actually worked.

Together they form the complete workforce availability model and become the operational input for future payroll, productivity analysis, overtime, shift management, and resource utilization across the entire ERP.
Now we reach one of the highest-volume entities in HR.
An enterprise with 5,000 employees may generate:
But it will generate millions of Attendance records over time.
This entity must be designed for performance, accuracy, and auditability.

sections.title: Attendance is the recorded presence, absence, or working status of an employee for a specific date and time according to organizational working schedules and attendance policies.
Responsibilities
paragraphs: It does not own leave balances.

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: Only one attendance record per employee per working day.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: AI becomes a workforce operations assistant.
"John has worked overtime for 18 consecutive business days and exceeds department averages."

sections.title: Attendance as the Workforce Activity Hub
🏛️ A Major Architectural Insight
paragraphs: HR now distinguishes three different concepts of time.
This separation is one of the hallmarks of enterprise ERP design.
Each concept is modeled independently without conflict.
lists: Be present and split time across multiple projects.

sections.title: One Refinement I'd Make
paragraphs: Rather than storing a single clock-in and clock-out pair, I'd make Attendance capable of supporting multiple attendance events.

The Attendance record remains the daily summary, while the underlying attendance events provide complete auditability and support biometric devices, multiple breaks, split shifts, and labor-law compliance.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next entity should be Performance Review.

sections.title: How well are they performing?
paragraphs: Performance Reviews will become the foundation for promotions, compensation adjustments, training plans, career development, succession planning, and long-term talent management—completing the HR Core before we move into advanced HR capabilities like Recruitment and Payroll.
This is the final core entity of Human Resources.
Everything we've built so far answers:
Now we answer the most important question.

sections.title: First Principle
paragraphs: A Performance Review is not a Performance Score.
The score is only one outcome.
The score is one small part.

sections.title: A Performance Review is a structured evaluation of an employee's work, behavior, achievements, competencies, and development during a defined review period, resulting in documented feedback, ratings, and future objectives.
Purpose
paragraphs: Performance Reviews become the foundation for:

sections.title: Goal Achievement
paragraphs: Future Goal entity can integrate here.

sections.title: Relationships
paragraphs: Performance becomes central to talent management.

sections.title: Business Rules
paragraphs: One review per employee per review period.

sections.title: AI Context
paragraphs: "Sarah has exceeded expectations for three consecutive annual reviews and demonstrates readiness for a Lead Engineer position."

sections.title: Goals Should Become Their Own Entity
Performance Review as the Talent Hub
Engineering Summary
paragraphs: Performance Review is not a score.

sections.title: 🏛️ What We've Built
paragraphs: HR is now a complete workforce management system.
Each entity has exactly one responsibility.
Every future HR capability naturally plugs into this foundation.

sections.title: One Architectural Refinement
paragraphs: I would introduce a future Performance Goal entity rather than embedding goals inside reviews.
That creates a continuous performance cycle:
This transforms performance management from a once-a-year event into an ongoing process.

sections.title: My Recommendation
paragraphs: The next major phase should be Document Management.
Every module we've built now creates documents:
Instead of every module storing files differently, we'll build a centralized Document Management layer that the entire ERP shares.
It becomes one of the most reusable and valuable infrastructure modules in KoreVity.
